content.title: About
content.content: Decaffeinated Cafe Mocha coffee is an aromatic beverage made from selected Arabica beans processed by a decaffeination method. It offers a rich chocolatey flavor and a smooth, creamy texture, perfect for those who want the taste of mocha without the stimulating effect of caffeine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The name “Mocha” originates from the Yemeni port city of Mocha, historically known for its fragrant coffee beans.
Decaffeination is usually performed by water or CO₂ processes, preserving most flavor compounds.
Decaf coffee contains roughly 2–5 mg of caffeine per serving, compared with 70–140 mg in regular espresso.
The combination of coffee and cocoa makes mocha a popular choice in cafés worldwide.
Decaf mocha is often used in desserts where coffee flavor is desired without caffeine overload.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Coffee provides polyphenols that help combat free radicals and support cellular health.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: While caffeine can irritate the stomach, the decaf version retains beneficial compounds without that effect.

items.title: May lower risk of certain diseases
items.content: Moderate coffee consumption, including decaf, has been linked to a reduced risk of type 2 diabetes and Parkinson’s disease.

items.title: Mood enhancement
items.content: Theobromine and other cocoa compounds present in mocha can contribute to improved mood.

items.title: Metabolism support
items.content: Although decaf coffee does not boost metabolism as strongly as regular coffee, it still contains compounds that modestly increase metabolic rate.

items.title: Allergy to coffee or cocoa
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to components of coffee or cocoa.

items.title: Acidic nature
items.content: Decaf coffee remains acidic and may irritate a sensitive stomach.

items.title: Additives and flavorings
items.content: Certain decaffeinated products may contain artificial flavorings; choose options without added chemicals.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use 1–2 teaspoons of ground decaf mocha with hot (not boiling) water at 90‑95 °C for 3‑4 minutes, then filter. Add milk, plant‑based milk, cream, or a touch of sugar as desired. Ideal for lattes, cappuccinos, and dessert sauces.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the coffee in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Avoid direct sunlight and moisture to preserve aroma and prevent oxidation.

flavored-rice-and-pasta-mixture-reduced-.title: Flavored Rice and Pasta Mixture, Reduced Sodium

content.title: About
content.content: The flavored rice and pasta mixture is a ready‑to‑cook blend that combines premium polished rice, small durum‑wheat pasta, and a blend of natural herbs and spices. The reduced‑sodium version contains 384 mg of sodium per serving, making it suitable for low‑salt diets.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The blend pairs two staple carbohydrate sources—rice and pasta—for lasting satiety.
Reduced sodium is achieved by using herbs and spices instead of added salt.
Preparation is simple: add hot water and let stand for 5‑7 minutes.
It uses whole‑grain rice rather than refined starch.
Suitable for vegetarians and, when gluten‑free pasta is used, for gluten‑free diets.

items.title: Energy source
items.content: Complex carbohydrates provide a quick, sustained source of energy for active individuals.

items.title: Low sodium
items.content: 384 mg of sodium per serving helps maintain normal blood pressure.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Rice and whole‑grain pasta contain thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Source of dietary fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain pasta and rice bran add fiber that promotes healthy digestion.

items.title: Contains minerals
items.content: The blend provides magnesium and phosphorus, important for bones and muscles.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: If regular pasta is used, the product may trigger reactions in people with wheat or gluten intolerance.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: The mixture can raise blood sugar quickly, so portion control is advised for diabetics.

items.title: Possible gluten cross‑contamination
items.content: Manufacturing facilities may have trace gluten, which is relevant for those with celiac disease.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Pour 250 ml of boiling water over the mix, stir, and let stand for 5‑7 minutes. Add vegetables, chicken breast, or legumes to boost protein. Finish with fresh herbs or a drizzle of olive oil if desired.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in a tightly sealed package. Follow the shelf‑life date on the label. Once opened, consume within 3‑4 weeks.

pizza-cheese-with-vegetables-from-restau.title: Pizza with cheese and vegetables, thick crust

content.title: About
content.content: Pizza with cheese and vegetables on a thick crust is a fast‑food dish made from dough topped with tomato sauce, melted cheese, and a variety of vegetables (tomatoes, bell peppers, onions, mushrooms, etc.). The dough forms a dense, crunchy crust while the topping stays juicy and flavorful.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Thin and thick crust pizzas differ in dough hydration and baking time.
Mozzarella cheese, commonly used on pizza, was first cultivated in Italy in the 12th century.
Adding vegetables makes the pizza more nutritious and lowers its calorie density compared to meat‑heavy versions.
Pizza gained massive popularity in the United States after World War II when American soldiers brought it back from Italy.
Traditional Neapolitan pizza is baked at 430–480 °C, but thick‑crust pizzas often use lower temperatures and longer bake times.

items.title: Rich source of calcium
items.content: The cheese provides calcium, essential for strong bones and teeth.

items.title: Vitamins and antioxidants
items.content: Vegetables such as tomatoes and peppers supply vitamin C and lycopene, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Protein
items.content: Cheese and some vegetables (e.g., peas) add both dairy and plant protein to the meal.

items.title: Dietary fiber
items.content: Vegetables and whole‑grain dough (if used) increase fiber content, supporting digestion.

items.title: Sustained energy
items.content: The thick crust provides complex carbohydrates that keep you feeling full longer.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Thick crust and cheese make the pizza calorie‑dense; portion control is advisable for weight‑management diets.

items.title: Saturated fats
items.content: Cheese contains saturated fats, which can raise cholesterol levels if consumed in excess.

items.title: Sodium
items.content: Tomato sauce and cheese are often salty, which may be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Milk protein allergy
items.content: Individuals allergic to dairy or lactose intolerant should choose dairy‑free cheese alternatives.

items.title: Gluten
items.content: Traditional dough contains gluten; those with celiac disease need a gluten‑free version.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the pizza hot, cut into slices. It pairs well with a light salad or a drizzle of chili sauce. Fresh herbs such as basil or oregano can be added after baking for extra aroma.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store leftovers in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2–3 days. Reheat in an oven or grill to keep the crust crisp.

content.title: About
content.content: A Popover is a floating container that appears over the current interface to provide additional information or a set of actions without navigating to a new page. It is commonly used for tooltips, quick forms, or context menus.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: A Popover can be attached to any UI element—button, icon, or text.
Unlike a modal dialog, a Popover does not block interaction with the rest of the page.
Many libraries offer automatic positioning based on available screen space.
Popovers are frequently used in mobile apps to save screen real estate.

items.title: Improved UX
items.content: Provides users with needed information quickly without leaving the current context.

items.title: Space Efficiency
items.content: Reduces the number of page navigations, simplifying navigation flows.

items.title: Customizable
items.content: Content, styling, and behavior can be tailored to specific use cases.

items.title: Responsive Design Support
items.content: Automatically adapts to different screen sizes, ensuring usability on mobile devices.

items.title: Interface Overload
items.content: Overusing Popovers can confuse users and degrade the overall experience.

items.title: Accessibility Issues
items.content: If not implemented with proper ARIA attributes, screen reader users may miss the Popover.

items.title: Closing Problems
items.content: Improper event handling may leave the Popover open unintentionally.

content.title: How to Use
content.content: Attach the Popover to a target element, define a trigger (click, hover), and specify its content—text, form, or action list. Ensure there is a clear way to close it, such as clicking outside or a close button.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Popover content is usually generated dynamically, but static templates can be cached in the browser memory for faster rendering.

potato-salad-made-with-light-creamy-dres.title: Potato Salad with Light Creamy Dressing

content.title: About
content.content: Potato salad with light creamy dressing is a classic dish popular in Russia and Eastern Europe. Boiled potatoes are cut into cubes and mixed with a light sour‑cream or yogurt‑based dressing, often flavored with mustard, dill and finely chopped onion.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The traditional recipe appeared in the early 20th century and quickly became a staple at festive tables.
The light dressing is usually made from sour cream, mayonnaise or yogurt, making the salad less heavy than versions with thick mayo.
Potatoes retain a good amount of vitamin C when not over‑cooked.
The salad is typically served cold, but some regions prefer it slightly warm to enhance herb aromas.
Variations may include boiled eggs, pickles or smoked salmon.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Potatoes provide slow‑release energy, helping to maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in vitamin C and potassium
items.content: These nutrients support immune function and healthy heart activity.

items.title: Low in saturated fat
items.content: A light creamy dressing usually contains less saturated fat than traditional mayonnaise.

items.title: Fiber from herbs
items.content: Dill and green onion add dietary fiber that aids digestion.

items.title: Supports gut microbiota
items.content: Using yogurt in the dressing introduces probiotics that can benefit intestinal health.

items.title: Dairy allergy
items.content: Cream or yogurt in the dressing may trigger reactions in people with lactose intolerance or milk allergy.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Potatoes can raise blood sugar quickly, so individuals with diabetes should monitor portion size.

items.title: Bacterial growth risk
items.content: If left at room temperature for more than 2 hours, the salad can become a breeding ground for bacteria.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: Dressings often contain added salt; those with hypertension should limit it.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the salad chilled as a side dish with meat, fish, or enjoy it as a light main course. Garnish with fresh herbs, sliced boiled eggs, or finely chopped pickles.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the salad in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. Stir before serving, as the dressing may settle. Discard if it develops an off‑odor or discoloration.

content.title: About
content.content: Puerto Rican white cheese is a soft fresh cheese made from cow’s milk. It has a mild creamy flavor with a slight saltiness and a characteristic white, slightly moist texture. The cheese is a staple in Caribbean cuisine, especially in dishes with rice, beans, and fried plantains.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The cheese takes its name from the island of Puerto Rico, where it was first produced in the early 20th century.
It is often served in small cubes or slices as a snack or salad topping.
Unlike aged cheeses, this fresh cheese is not aged and is meant to be consumed within a few days of production.
It is a key ingredient in the traditional dish “mojito con queso,” where it adds a creamy texture.
In many Spanish‑speaking regions it is simply called “queso blanco” – “white cheese.”

items.title: Rich in calcium
items.content: Calcium supports bone and tooth health.

items.title: Source of protein
items.content: Casein protein helps maintain muscle mass.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Compared with aged cheeses, it contains less saturated fat.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Provides vitamin B12 and riboflavin, important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Probiotic potential
items.content: Fresh cheese may contain live lactic‑acid bacteria that support gut microbiota.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains lactose, so people with intolerance should limit intake.

items.title: Milk‑protein allergy
items.content: Some individuals may react to casein.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: The cheese is often salted; those monitoring sodium should take this into account.

items.title: Shelf life
items.content: High moisture means it spoils quickly; store properly and consume within a few days.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Eat the cheese fresh, cubed in salads, added to tacos, baked in casseroles, or used as a sandwich filling. It is also commonly paired with mango, avocado, or lime.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the cheese refrigerated at 2‑4 °C, wrapped in plastic film or in an airtight container. For longer storage (over a week) it can be frozen, though the texture may change.

content.title: About
content.content: The tuna salad wrap is a convenient handheld meal made of tender tuna, mayonnaise, fresh vegetables and herbs rolled inside a soft flatbread. It is commonly served in fast‑casual eateries and as a ready‑to‑eat lunch option.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tuna is one of the most widely consumed seafoods worldwide, harvested from both wild fisheries and aquaculture.
The tuna salad wrap originated in the United States in the 1970s as a portable alternative to the classic sandwich.
The flatbread used is typically a whole‑wheat tortilla made without yeast, giving it a mild flavor and flexible texture.
The combination of tuna and mayo provides a balanced mix of protein and fat, making the wrap both satisfying and energy‑dense.
Some versions add avocado, boosting the content of heart‑healthy monounsaturated fats.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Tuna supplies high‑quality protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Omega‑3 fatty acids
items.content: EPA and DHA in tuna support cardiovascular health and brain function.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Tuna provides B12, niacin and B6, which are important for energy metabolism.

items.title: Minerals
items.content: Tuna contains selenium, magnesium and potassium, contributing to nerve function and blood pressure regulation.

items.title: Fiber from vegetables
items.content: The lettuce, tomato and cucumber add dietary fiber, aiding digestion.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to tuna.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared wraps often contain added salt and sauces, which can be a concern for people with hypertension.

items.title: Mercury
items.content: Tuna can contain trace amounts of mercury; intake should be limited for children and pregnant women.

items.title: Calorie‑dense mayo
items.content: Mayonnaise adds significant calories and fat, so lighter versions are advisable.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The wrap is eaten by hand, usually cut in half. Serve with a light yogurt‑based or mustard sauce. Optional toppings include avocado slices, olives or a squeeze of fresh lemon juice.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep the wrap in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 2‑3 days. For longer storage, freeze it and thaw in the fridge before eating.
